extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced geometry students (readers of The Mathematician journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Determine when plane sections of a general second-degree surface (quadric) are circles; classify which quadrics admit real/imaginary series of circular sections and the orientations of those planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 80 method constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Note. This exercise is to be solved by the principles of arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposer explicitly restricts acceptable solution methods: use arithmetic principles rather than algebraic/analytical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: General representation of a second-degree surface and family through intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: It is well known that the general equation to surfaces of the second degree can always be reduced to the form w = Ax^2 + By^2 + Cz^2 + Dx + Ey + Fz + G, and if the equations of two planes cutting the surface are ?? = a x + β y + γ z + 1 = 0, and ??' = a' x + β' y + γ' z + 1 = 0, the equation to a surface of the second degree passing through the two curves of intersection will be u = m v v', m being an arbitrary constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the algebraic framework used to derive conditions for circular sections: express a surface through the product m·(plane1)·(plane2) and compare coefficients to obtain necessary equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic conditions for the plane-section surface {c} to be a sphere (i.e., circular section family)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions in order that the surface {c} may be a sphere, are maa — A = mpp' — B = m77' — C, and the off-diagonal/coefficient cross-sum conditions aβ' + a'β = 0, βγ' + β'γ = 0, γa' + γ' a = 0 (these last three may be inconsistent in general unless some of the coefficients vanish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By expanding u = m v v' and equating with quadratic form coefficients one obtains these necessary algebraic relations; special assumptions (e.g., a = 0, a' = 0, or β = 0, β' = 0, etc.) lead to reduced systems and families of circular sections with some parameters indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: General fact: six series of circular sections (real or imaginary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equations (61), (62), and (63) show that in general every surface of the second degree has six series of circular sections (real or imaginary) parallel to the three principal axes of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: for a general quadric there are up to six families (two for each principal axis direction) of plane-parallel sections that are (possibly imaginary) circles; determining which are real depends on sign/order of principal coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of linear and constant terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of the planes of the circular sections is obviously independent of the coefficients D, E, F, and the absolute term G of the quadratic equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the quadratic (principal) part determines the directions and existence of circular-section families; translations (linear terms) and constant term do not affect the orientation of such planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case I — Ellipsoid: two series of real circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Case I. When the given surface is an ellipsoid, by taking its principal axes as axes of coordinates equation (a) becomes Ax^2 + By^2 + Cz^2 = 1; hence A, B, C are positive; and if A < B < C, equations (62) are real, but (61) and (63) are imaginary: consequently the equations indicate two series of real circular sections, parallel to the axis of y, or to the mean axis of the ellipsoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion: an ellipsoid (with ordered principal coefficients) admits two real families of circular sections; which family is real depends on the ordering of A,B,C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case II — Hyperboloid of one sheet: two series of real circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Case II. When the surface (a) is a hyperboloid of one sheet, by referring the surface to its principal axes equation becomes (principal form) hence C is negative, and if A < B equations (62) give real results but (61) and (63) give imaginary: hence the hyperboloid of one sheet has only two series of real circular sections, which are both parallel to the greater axis of the principal elliptic section, or to the greater real axis of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hyperboloid of one sheet admits two real circular-section families aligned with its larger principal axis; other candidate families are imaginary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case III — Hyperboloid of two sheets: two series of real circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Case III. When the surface (a) is a hyperboloid of two sheets, its equation may be reduced to the form (principal form) hence if B < C equations (62) give the real results but (61) and (63) are imaginary: hence this surface has only two series of circular sections, the planes of which are both parallel to the axis of y, or the greater imaginary axis of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again two real families exist (orientation depends on coefficient ordering); the remaining families are imaginary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case IV — Elliptic paraboloid: two series of circular sections (real)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case IV. When the given surface is an elliptic paraboloid, taking axis as z and principal diametral planes xz and yz yields A = 0, and if B < C equations (62) give real results but (61) and (63) are imaginary: hence the elliptic paraboloid has two series of circular sections, both parallel to the axis of y, which lies in the plane of the principal parabolic section whose parameter is the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An elliptic paraboloid admits two real series of circular sections parallel to one principal direction; which depends on relative sizes of the paraboloid's principal parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case V — Hyperbolic paraboloid: two series but circles degenerate to straight lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Case V. When the surface is a hyperbolic paraboloid ... equations (62) give real results but (61) and (63) are imaginary. These equations indicate two series of circular sections parallel to the principal axis of the surface. In this case however each of the circles degenerates into a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although algebraic conditions produce 'circular' families, geometric degeneration causes the intersections to be straight lines rather than true circles; check projections on coordinate planes to see degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case VI — Cone: two series of circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Case VI. When the given surface is a cone, by referring it to its principal axes the equation becomes kx^2 + By^2 - Cz^2 = 0, hence when A < B equations (61) give real results but (62) and (63) are imaginary: therefore the cone has two series of circular sections, parallel to the axis of x, or to the greater axis of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cone admits two families of circular cross-sections in planes parallel to the axis associated with the larger principal coefficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case VII — Elliptic cylinder: two series of circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Case VII. When the given surface is an elliptic cylinder ... equation becomes Ax^2 + By^2 = 1, hence if A < B equation (61) gives real but (62) and (63) imaginary: hence the surface has two series of circular sections parallel to the greater axis of the principal section of the cylinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elliptic cylinder: circular sections occur in two parallel-plane families orthogonal to the cylinder axis, determined by coefficient ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case VIII — Hyperbolic cylinder: indicated circles degenerate to lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Case VIII. When the given surface is a hyperbolic cylinder ... equations (62) give real results but (61) and (63) give imaginary results. These equations appear to indicate two series of circular sections, but it may be shown as in the fifth case, that the circles degenerate into straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although algebraic solutions suggest 'circular' families, geometrically the intersections in this hyperbolic-cylinder case are straight lines (degenerate circles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case IX — Parabolic cylinder: every section perpendicular to axis is a (degenerate) circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Case IX. When the given surface is a parabolic cylinder, equation may be reduced to By^2 - x = 1; hence equations (62) give y + ... = 0. Equations (63) give the same result, and (61) are imaginary. Hence it appears that every section by a plane perpendicular to the axis of z is a circle; but the circle in all cases degenerates into a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a parabolic cylinder the 'circular' sections perpendicular to the axis are algebraically indicated but geometrically degenerate into straight lines.
